```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(psych) # Omega
library(lavaan) # CFA analysis
library(mirt) # IRT analysis
library(ggplot2)
library(ggiraph) # interactive plot
library(corrplot) #corrplot
library(htmlwidgets) # interaction online
```

```{r}
data = read.csv("International_vaiak.csv")
```

# Art Interest

```{r}
data_ai = data %>%
  filter(
    if_any(AI_1_1:AI_2_4, ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
  mutate(
    Expertise = factor(ArtExp_Expertise_cluster))
```

This graph represent the distribution of the score of the AI scale

```{r}

data_ai_score = data_ai %>%
  count(Art_Interest, name = "n") %>%
  filter(!is.na(Art_Interest))

graph_ai = ggplot(data_ai_score, aes(y = n, x = Art_Interest,
                                tooltip = paste0(Art_Interest, ": ", n), 
                                data_id = Art_Interest)) +
  geom_col_interactive(fill = "grey70",
                        hover_css = "fill:#009b64; 
                       stroke:black; 
                       stroke-width:1.5px;") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Variable : Art Interest distribution")  +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none")

girafe(ggobj = graph_ai) 
```

## Internal reliability

```{r, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
omega_ai = data_ai %>%                              # Omega analysis Art Interest
  select(starts_with("AI")) %>%
  omega
```

The McDonald's omega indicate a good internal reliability

```{r}
omega_ai$omega.tot
```

## Confirmatory factor analysis

### One factor model

Firstly I will carry a one factor model with the additional correlation that we established before.

```{r}
Model_AI_one = "interest  =~ AI_1_1 + AI_1_2 + AI_1_3 + AI_1_4 + AI_1_5 + AI_1_6 + AI_1_7 +
                       
                           AI_2_1 + AI_2_2 + AI_2_3 + AI_2_4

                           AI_1_3 ~~ AI_1_7
                           AI_2_2 ~~ AI_2_4" 

AI_onefactor = cfa(Model_AI_one, data = data_ai, std.lv=TRUE, estimator = "MLR")  # CFA with MLR

fitMeasures(AI_onefactor, c(
  "chisq",
  "df",
  "pvalue",
  "cfi",
  "tli",
  "rmsea",
  "rmsea.ci.lower",
  "rmsea.ci.upper",
  "rmsea.pvalue",
  "srmr"))    # Indices
```

The CFI, TLI and SRMR indicate a good fit, while the RMSEA is above the general accepted value.

Thus, I analysed the correlation between the residuals

```{r}
residuals = residuals(AI_onefactor, type = "cor") # residuals

residuals = residuals$cov

corrplot(residuals,
         method = "color",
         type = "upper",
         col.lim = c(-0.4, 0.4))
```

### Two factor model

I proposed a different model, where the two parts of the scale are two separate factors (interest_subjective and interest_behaviour) with a hierchical higher factor (interest).

```{r}
Model_AI_two = "interest_subj =~ AI_1_1 + AI_1_2 + AI_1_3 + AI_1_4 + AI_1_5 + AI_1_6 + AI_1_7

                interest_beha =~ AI_2_1 + AI_2_2 + AI_2_3 + AI_2_4 

                interest =~ interest_subj + interest_beha" # model

AI_twofactor = cfa(Model_AI_two, data = data_ai, std.lv=TRUE, estimator = "MLR")  # CFA with MLR

fitMeasures(AI_twofactor, c(
  "chisq",
  "df",
  "pvalue",
  "cfi",
  "tli",
  "rmsea",
  "rmsea.ci.lower",
  "rmsea.ci.upper",
  "rmsea.pvalue",
  "srmr"))    # Indices
```

The indexes all improved, the RMSEA is still above the criteria.

## Item Responce Theory

### Full scale results

```{r, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
AI = data_ai %>% 
  select(starts_with("AI"))

AI_grm = mirt(AI, 1, itemtype = "graded") # run the model

coef = coef(AI_grm, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE) # item parameters
```

This graph represent how informative is the questionnaire compared to the ability of the participants ($\theta$).

```{r}
theta = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)

test_info = testinfo(AI_grm, Theta = theta)

df = data.frame(
  theta = theta, 
  information = test_info)

ggplot(df, aes(x = theta, y=information)) +
  geom_line(color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
      scale_fill_manual(values=c("black")) +
  ylim(0, 25) +
  theme_bw(18) + 
  theme(panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA),
        text = element_text(family = "sourcesans"),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(0.4, "cm"), 
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 15, color = "black"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15, color = "black"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 20), 
        legend.position = c(0.20, 0.7),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 14), 
        legend.title = element_text(size = 14), 
        legend.background = element_rect(
          color = "black",  
          linetype = "solid"))
```

We can notice that it is in general pretty normally distributed around 0, with a limited skewness into the lower values.

### Individual items

For each item, $a$ represents the discrimination parameter, how much the value vary in relation to the ability $\theta$. A high $a$ means that the probability of answering an item correctly changes very sharply as $\theta$ increases.

```{r}
coef_item = coef$items

data.frame(a = coef_item[, 1])
```

$b$ represents the how much ability the participants needs to pass from an asnwer to the next. For example, for item AI_1_1, participants has a 50% probability of responding with an ability to at least 0.08541134 (b5) to answer 6 or higher. The higher the $b$ the more difficult it is.

```{r}
data.frame(coef_item[, 2:7])
```

The graph represents this data. Each box is an item and each line represents the probability to answer in a specific way (P1 probability to answer 1). The slope of the lines represent the $a$, the steeper it is, the higher $a$ is, the more efficient is the question in distinguish between individuals who know the material and those who do not.

```{r}
plot(AI_grm, type = "trace", 
     facet_items = TRUE) # ICCs and category functioning
```

Subsequentially we check how much the factor (Art Interest) is linked to the item. $F1$ represents the factor loading, while $h2$ is how much variability of the item is explained by the factor.

```{r}
summary(AI_grm) # threshold check
```

## Distribution

```{r}
summary_ai_exp = data_ai %>%
  group_by(Expertise) %>%
  summarise(
    n_participants = n(),
    male_count     = sum(Dem_Gender == "Male",   na.rm = TRUE),
    female_count   = sum(Dem_Gender == "Female", na.rm = TRUE),
    other_count    = sum(!(Dem_Gender %in% c("Male","Female")), na.rm = TRUE), 
    art_interest = mean(Art_Interest, na.rm = TRUE), 
    art_interest_sd = sd(Art_Interest, na.rm = TRUE))

graph_density = ggplot(
  data_ai,
  aes(
    x = Art_Interest, 
    tooltip = Expertise,
    data_id = Expertise)) +
    xlim(0, 88) +
  ylim(-0.00, 0.05) +
  labs(x = "Art Interest", y = "Density", fill="Expertise") +
  geom_density_interactive(
    fill = "gray70",
    alpha = 0.6,
    colour = "gray40",
    hover_css = "fill:#ffb600; stroke:black;") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(0.4, "cm"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 20, color = "black"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 20), 
        plot.title = element_text(size = 20),
        legend.position = "none",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 15), 
        legend.title = element_text(size = 18), 
        legend.background = element_rect(
          color = "black",  
          linetype = "solid")) +
  ggtitle("Art Interest density plot")

girafe(ggobj = graph_density) 

knitr::kable(
  summary_ai_exp %>%
  select(Expertise, n_participants, art_interest, art_interest_sd), 
  col.names = c("Group", "Number of participants", "Mean", "SD"),
  digits = 2, 
  align = "c")
```
